profile.summary: BERTax reads a DNA sequence and says which part of the tree of life it came from, without comparing it to a database of known genomes. It is a BERT model: the sequence is cut into overlapping three letter tokens and a transformer encoder reads them, and classification layers on top predict superkingdom, phylum and, in the released version, genus. The point of the method is novel organisms: when no close relative exists in a reference database, similarity search degrades, while BERTax works from the statistics of the sequence itself.

summary_quotes.text: Here we present BERTax, a deep neural network program based on natural language processing to precisely classify the superkingdom and phylum of DNA sequences taxonomically without the need for a known representative relative from a database.
Each sequence was split into 500 3-mers (i.e., tokens in a natural language), with the first 250 3-mers being the first sentence and the second 250 3-mers being the second sentence
The script takes a (multi)fasta as input and outputs a list of predicted classes to the console:

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Training has two steps. First a BERT encoder is pretrained without labels on genomic fragments of a fixed length of 1,500 nucleotides, each cut into 500 three letter tokens and presented as two sentences of 250 tokens. Then the model is fine-tuned for classification: the [CLS] token output goes to three taxonomy layers in what the authors call the all-in-one architecture, where each rank's prediction also sees the higher ranks. The authors compared flat, nested and all-in-one arrangements and found all-in-one best. Fine-tuning ran for at most 16 epochs with early stopping, and class weights per rank to stop the model favouring frequent classes. At prediction time each rank also has an unknown class, used when a sequence looks unlike any trained class.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Pretraining and Architectures, Results; README.md: Usage note on unknown

quotes.text: To model DNA as natural language, BERTax was pretrained on DNA sequences of a fixed length of 1,500 nucleotides.

The taxonomy layers use our all-in-one architecture which uses the output of the pretrained BERT model and all higher taxonomic ranks to predict superkingdom, phylum, and—only in the final model—also the genus of an input sequence.
We developed three different DNN architectures: the 1) flat, 2) nested, and 3) all-in-one architectures, which we compared with each other.
We fine-tuned all models for a maximum of 16 epochs, employing early stopping
Note, that "unknown" is a special placeholder class for each prediction rank, meaning the sequence's taxonomy is predicted to be unlike any possible output class.

sections.title: What it can classify
sections.body: Four superkingdoms (archaea, bacteria, eukaryota and viruses), and a fixed list of phyla and genera that the README prints without giving counts. Anything outside those lists is likely to come back as unknown, and the authors say so plainly. The README also carries their recommendation to use BERTax for superkingdom and phylum, with genus possible but weaker, and points at the separate training repository for building a model that covers other taxa.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Compatible phyla and genera, Training BERTax models; Paper: Introduction

quotes.text: Due to the limited amount of samples that can be used for training, we could not train all known phyla and genera.
If the taxon of your sample is not included in this list, there is a high probability that phylum/genus will be predicted as "unknown".
Note: We recommend using BERTax only for super kingdom and phylum prediction, but genera are possible.
Here, we present the tool BERTax for classification of DNA sequences on three different taxonomic levels, superkingdom (archaea, bacteria, eukaryota, and viruses), phylum, and genus.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The published tool is one model: the downloadable version, built on the all-in-one architecture, trained on what the paper calls the final model dataset, and the only version that predicts genus as well. The weights are a single file, big_trainingset_all_fix_classes_selection.h5, distributed through the repository's latest release, and the tool is also packaged as a conda package and a Docker image. The paper additionally describes models trained on a closely related and a distantly related dataset, used for its comparisons; those are not the released tool. A result should name the model file, the sequence splitting mode and the window settings, since long sequences are chunked and the chunk predictions are averaged by default.

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: BERT transformer encoder with self-attention over 3-mer tokens, plus three taxonomy layers in the all-in-one arrangement, where each rank's output also uses the higher ranks. Only the [CLS] token is passed from the encoder to the taxonomy layers.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Architectures; Figure 1 description

quotes.text: BERTax is based on the DNN encoder architecture BERT, that relies on a transformer employing the mechanism of self-attention
The pretrained transformation blocks process this input, and only the [CLS] token is delivered to the taxonomy layers as output

The taxonomy layers use our all-in-one architecture which uses the output of the pretrained BERT model and all higher taxonomic ranks to predict superkingdom, phylum, and—only in the final model—also the genus of an input sequence.

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: A fasta or multifasta file of DNA sequences. Internally a sequence is tokenised into 3-mers over a window of 1,500 nucleotides; longer sequences are split into equal chunks by default, or sampled with a single random window, or scanned with a running window.

facts.label: Training data
facts.value: Pretraining: 1 million genomic fragments of 1,500 nt for each of the four superkingdoms, from NCBI RefSeq genomes. Fine-tuning: the paper's datasets, with the released model trained on the final model dataset, an expanded closely related dataset with roughly tripled eukaryotic and bacterial fragment counts. run_guide.summary: Classify the sequences in a fasta file with the released BERTax model, either through Docker or through a local install.
prerequisites: Docker, for the route the README puts first. For GPU use, the nvidia-container-toolkit and the --gpus all flag.
Or conda, for a local install from the fkretschmer channel, plus pip for keras-bert 0.86.0.
For the pip only route, the model file big_trainingset_all_fix_classes_selection.h5 from the repository's latest release, placed in the resources subfolder.
A fasta or multifasta file of DNA sequences.

steps.title: Run with Docker
steps.explanation: The README's first route: it pulls and runs the published image, with your input directory mounted at /in. Add --gpus all to use a GPU, which the README says is likely much faster.

quotes.text: docker run -t --rm -v /path/to/input/files:/in fkre/bertax:latest /in/sequences.fa
the `bertax` image has to be run with the flag `--gpus all`

notes: The official repository is rnajena/bertax, which the paper's own README identifies and whose GitHub licence field is GPL-3.0. The record's attributes name github.com/f-kretschmer/bertax instead; that address was not checked, and the conda channel in the README is fkretschmer, so the record may be recording the author's name rather than the repository owner. The record's existing source, the PNAS paper, was fetched in full from PMC; it carries a CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 licence, so store_bytes is false for it. The paper also describes models trained on closely related and distantly related datasets, which are evaluation models rather than the released tool, and a separate training repository (rnajena/bertax_training) that was not fetched.
